newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank accounts set for revamp ahead of EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank accounts set for revamp ahead of EMU.

text.p: Germany's fiercely-independent central bank on Thursday looked set to undergo sweeping changes in its accounts after the German Finance Ministry presented plans for reform in the run-up to European Monetary Union.

In a brief two-sentence statement, the powerful Bundesbank gave no specifics about the planned changes. But government sources said these would include a revaluation of at least some central bank assets to bring them closer to market value.

"With respect to the principles envisioned for accounting within the European System of Central Banks, Finance Minister Theo Waigel and State Secretary Juergen Stark presented initial thoughts on changes to some definitions on accounting principles in the Bundesbank law and conducted an initial exchange of views with the members of the central bank council at the meeting," the Bundesbank statement said.
"The central bank council's discussions will be continued soon on the basis of a draft paper which will be drawn up by the German Finance Ministry," it added.

Germany, once the star candidate for EMU membership, is seeking desperately to rein in its budget deficits to three percent of gross domestic product or less to make sure it qualifies fairly and squarely for entry to the euro in 1999.
The issue took on a new urgency on Thurday as experts from federal, state and local governments announced an additional shortfall of 18 billion marks in estimated 1997 tax revenues.
Germany's forecast of a 2.9 percent deficit this year is already seen as utopic by many independent analysts.
The talk of gold sales and asset revaluation follows the announcement on Wednesday that Bonn is considering an earlier sale of some of its Deutsche Telekom shares.

A Finance Ministry spokeswoman said on Thursday in response to Reuter enquiries that Germany had no plans to sell gold to aid the federal budget and also had no plans to make any such recommendation to the Bundesbank.
But both the finance ministry and the central bank declined to be drawn on whether a revaluation of the assets was planned in a bid to avert a mid-year rise in indirect taxes.

Coalition sources confirmed to Reuters that plans have been drawn up in this direction. Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) are particularly opposed to an increase in indirect taxation to top up budget coffers.
The Bundesbank currently books its assets at their all-time lowest price or at the purchase price, a method which is normal under German bookkeeping regulations.

A revaluation could thus bring a huge windfall profit to the bank -- and thus to Bonn. In gold alone, the Bundesbank holds 95 million ounces originally acquired at an average price of 144 marks an ounce, for a total value of 13.7 billion marks.
At the current market value of about 600 marks an ounce, it would be worth about 57 billion marks.

Yet even if Bonn could succeed in freeing up the funds tied up in the central bank's 95 million ounces of gold, it was not immediately clear how or whether these could be used to help Germany in its efforts to meet the Maastricht criteria.

Sources said an outright sale of gold to realise the assets appeared unlikely, given the fact that Germany has led a vocal campaign of opposition to sales of only a small proportion of the International Monetary Fund's gold assets.

A simple revaluation of the assets to a higher value closer to the market price -- although it is technically allowed under German bookkeeping laws -- would mark a change from the established practice. One source said this could even require a change in the Bundesbank law.
Even once those assets are revalued, it is unclear how the resultant extraordinary profit could be transferred to Bonn in a way which would genuinely help the deficit to be reduced.
Conventionally, Bonn uses any profit over a budgeted amount of seven billion marks to retire old debt. It need not necessarily use a special profit in this way.
But a transfer of that money to the cover the budget deficit would likely run into problems when it comes to the assessment of which country meets the Maastricht criteria.

The acting director of Eurostat, Daniel Byk, declined to comment on this specific case, but noted that European Union (EU) rules stating that a nation cannot reduce its deficit through central bank gold sales applied to all EU nations.
"The rules apply to all countries," Byk told Reuters in response to a question on whether Bonn could legitimately sell Bundesbank gold to help reduce its budget deficit.
EU rules state gold sales from central banks can be used only to reduce the government debt, but not to cut the deficit.

A further monetary source, commenting directly on the German case, said in his view the EU rules would not allow a government to revalue a central bank's gold reserves and book the increased value into the budget to reduce the deficit.
